The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+1\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-4)\cdot {C}_{22}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =(-4)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(2+3)+2(1+6) \\  & =-20+14 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.
$$
